title: Cabral's Fleet to Brazil and India
intro: King Manuel I of Portugal sent a fleet of 13 ships and 1500 men under Pedro Álvares Cabral to India to secure a treaty with Calicut, find Sofala and bring back spices. On the way the fleet reached the coast of Brazil, where the Tupiniquim lived.
ending: Cabral reached Lisbon on 21 July 1501 with the treaty with Calicut unmade and the war with it begun. Of the 13 ships, five were lost, and Portugal gained a factory in Cochin and a claim to Brazil.

legs.title: Lisbon to the coast of Brazil

stops.text: The fleet set out from the Tagus, the river of Lisbon. It was a large, well-armed armada of 13 ships and 1500 men, carrying gifts and letters for the rulers of the east.
stops.quote: On March 9, Cabral's expedition set out from the Tagus.

stops.text: The fleet reached the island in the middle of a storm. The ship of Luís Pires was too damaged by the tempest to go on and returned to Lisbon.
stops.quote: Thirteen days later, on March 22, Cabral's armada reached the island of São Nicolau in the middle of a storm.

stops.text: After 44 days from departure the fleet sighted the coast of Brazil and named a hill Monte Pascoal. Tupiniquim people gathered on the beach, but the surf was too strong for a landing.
stops.quote: The next day, the armada caught sight of the Brazilian coast, seeing the outlines of a hill they named Monte Pascoal.

stops.text: The fleet sheltered behind the reef at Cabrália Bay, near Porto Seguro. Friar Henrique Soares held a mass before 200 Tupiniquim on 26 April. On 1 May Cabral claimed the land for Portugal as the Ilha de Vera Cruz and left a couple of convicts with the Tupiniquim.
stops.quote: Strong overnight winds prompted the armada to lift anchor and sail some 10 leagues (45 km) north, finding harbor behind the reef at Cabrália Bay, just north of Porto Seguro.

legs.title: Round the Cape and up the East African coast

stops.text: The fleet met headlong winds for six days at the Cape. Four ships, among them that of Bartolomeu Dias, were lost at sea, which left seven.
stops.quote: After crossing the Atlantic Ocean, Cabral's armada reached the Cape of Good Hope in late May.

stops.text: Cabral's three-ship squadron chased two merchant ships. One ran aground and the other was captured, then released when it proved to belong to a cousin of the sultan of Malindi.
stops.quote: On June 16, 1500, Cabral's three-ship squadron reached the Primeiras Islands several leagues north of Sofala.

stops.text: The Sultan of Mozambique gave Cabral a warm reception and let him collect water and supplies. Three more ships joined him here, and the fleet went on with six ships.
stops.quote: The three ships landed on Mozambique Island on June 22.

stops.text: Cabral met Emir Ibrahim in rowboats in the harbour and offered a treaty from King Manuel I. Ibrahim was suspicious, and Cabral, worried about missing the monsoon, broke off the talks and sailed on.
stops.quote: More than a month later, on July 26, Cabral's armada reached Kilwa, the dominant city-state of the East African coast and which Gama had never visited.

stops.text: After avoiding hostile Mombasa, the fleet was well received by the Sultan of Malindi. Cabral landed the Malindi ambassador, took on two Gujarati pilots and crossed the Indian Ocean from 7 August.
stops.quote: Pressing north, the Cabral fleet avoided the hostile Mombassa (Mombaça) and finally reached friendly Malindi (Melinde) on August 2.

stops.text: After an uneventful crossing the six ships rested, and were repaired and repainted.
stops.quote: After an uneventful ocean crossing, Cabral's six ships landed on Anjediva Island (Angediva, Anjadip) on August 22, where they rested and repaired and repainted the ships.

stops.text: Cabral went ashore only after hostages were exchanged, and met the Zamorin. A trade treaty was agreed and the Portuguese were allowed a factory, where Aires Correia landed with around 70 men.
stops.quote: Sailing down the Indian coast, Cabral's expedition finally reached Calicut on September 13.

stops.text: Cabral seized an Arab merchant ship, and a mob attacked the factory. 53 Portuguese were killed (some sources say 70). Cabral then seized about ten Arab ships, killed their crews, burned them and bombarded the city for a day, with casualties of up to 600.
stops.quote: Incensed, the Arab merchants around the quay immediately raised a riot in Calicut and direct mobs to attack the Portuguese factory.

stops.text: On the advice of Gaspar da Gama, Cabral sailed to Cochin, a rival of Calicut. He made an alliance with its raja against Calicut, and a Portuguese factory was set up under Gonçalo Gil Barbosa.
stops.quote: At the suggestion of Gaspar da Gama, the Goese Jew who had been accompanying the expedition, Cabral set sail south along the coast toward Cochin kingdom

stops.text: Cabral loaded cargo at the declining city and met its Malabari Jewish and Syrian Christian communities. Two Syrian Christian priests asked for passage to Europe.
stops.quote: Finding the supply in Cochin running low, Cabral took up the offer to load some cargo at Cranganore.

stops.text: After leaving Cochin when news came of a Calicut fleet of around 80 boats, Cabral swung wide of Calicut and was received by the Kolathiri Raja, who sold spices on credit. Cabral paid him all the same.
stops.quote: Heading north, Cabral's armada took a wide sweep to avoid Calicut, and paid a quick visit to Cannanore.

stops.text: Vice-admiral Sancho de Tovar ran the spice-laden El Rei aground on the Malindi coast. The ship could not be repaired, so its crew and cargo were reallocated and it was burnt for its iron fittings.
stops.quote: As Cabral's expedition approached Malindi in February, vice-admiral Sancho de Tovar, sailing at the front, ran his spice-laden ship, the El Rei, aground on the Malindi coast.

stops.text: With five ships left and no news of Diogo Dias, Cabral sent the fast Anunciada ahead under Nicolau Coelho and sent Tovar in the São Pedro to find Sofala.
stops.quote: Cabral's fleet, reduced to just five ships, reached Mozambique Island in the spring.

stops.text: At the bay of Dakar, called Bezeguiche, Cabral found Diogo Dias and Nicolau Coelho waiting. Pêro de Ataíde and Tovar arrived by the end of June.
stops.quote: Shortly after, Cabral and Simão de Miranda themselves reached Bezeguiche, where they find Diogo Dias and Nicolau Coelho awaiting them.

stops.text: Cabral and Miranda arrived in Lisbon a month after Coelho. Tovar and Ataíde followed on 25 July and Dias, with his empty caravel, on 27 July.
stops.quote: One month after Coelho's arrival, on July 21, Cabral and Miranda, captaining the two larger ships, finally arrived in Lisbon.

notes: Calicut appears twice because the fleet stayed there from September to December (not a return). The Cabrália Bay date is only April 1500 (article gives days for events around it, not the move); the 26 April mass and 1 May claim are from lines beside the quote. Wp for Cabrália Bay is Santa Cruz Cabrália (municipality); Primeiras Islands wp is the archipelago; Bezeguiche is Dakar's bay per the article. The Frade river anchorage (23 April) was left out as a river. The article says the Zamorin 'new' vs Gama; casualties at Calicut 53 (some say 70), up to 600 from the bombardment. Left out: Cochin departure 16 January (leaving only), Diogo Dias's separate voyage, Sofala (seen from afar only). Article uses 'discovered' for Brazil; text says sighted. Tupiniquim named as in article. Mozambique Island 'spring' and Malindi 'February' dates from 1501.
